newsitem.title: LEBANON: Demand for dollars up in Beirut.
newsitem.headline: Demand for dollars up in Beirut.

text.p: Tight allocations of shorter-term Lebanese-pound treasury bills by the central bank helped boost demand for U.S. dollars on the Beirut foreign exchange market in the week ended on Friday, dealers said.
The dollar traded near the middle of the central bank's bid-offer intervention band after hovering near the bottom of the band in recent weeks.
The central bank lowered the band during the week to 1,535.50-1,545 Lebanese pounds from 1,536-1,545.50.
But dealers said the dollar traded in inter-bank trade at between 1,538 and 1,541 pounds compared with 1,536 to 1,537.5 pounds last week.

"Demand for dollars is a little bit more than supply...We are dealing above the central bank's buying rate and of course nobody is selling dollars to the central bank," a dealer who asked not to be identified told Reuters.
"Maybe it is because the allocation of short-term t-bills is so small. The Banque du Liban is not giving people as much as they want," he said.
"There is also some commercial demand for dollars and not much supply."

The central bank's restriction on sales of three-and six-month t-bills, which are denominated in Lebanese pounds, increased demand for dollars because investors were only allowed to buy very small proportions of the amount they bid for, and so were changing their excess funds back into dollars, the dealer said.
At its last weekly t-bill auction on June 12 the central bank restricted acceptance of bids for three-month and six-month bills to three percent and 10 percent respectively.
